title: How A Simple Question Can Be A Powerful Motivator motivator/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin critiques the standard 'Are there any questions?' check-for-understanding, noting it disproportionately draws responses from already-attentive, high-achieving students while leaving disengaged students silent even when confused. His proposed fix is to flip the question into a negative form—'Is there anyone who doesn't know what to do?'—which he argues more directly targets inattentive or unsure students by making them self-check their readiness. Linsin explains the strategy has a dual benefit: students grow more attentive because they know they'll be asked a challenging question, and confused students are more likely to raise their hand for a genuinely necessary clarification. He notes this technique requires the teacher's visible attention throughout the activity to be fully effective, and offers several other example phrasings for different situations.
points: The common check-for-understanding question ('Are there any questions?') disproportionately draws responses from already-attentive, motivated students.
Linsin's fix is to flip the phrasing into a negative form ('Is there anyone who doesn't know what to do?'), which targets disengaged or unsure students more directly.
The negative-question technique produces two benefits: increased overall attentiveness in anticipation of being challenged, and more genuine clarifying questions from students who need help.
For full effectiveness, the strategy requires the teacher's sustained visible attention on the class during the activity, not multitasking or turning away.
The technique is adaptable to multiple situations, such as checking readiness for homework, recess rules, or an upcoming test.
quotes: After giving directions, it’s common for teachers to ask, “Are there any questions?
The rest of your class, those who most need to consider your question, are unlikely to say a word—even if they have no idea what you expect them to do.
This question effectively skips past the high-achievers—who will almost never respond to it—and lands directly in the laps of those who urgently need it.
First, when students grow accustomed to you asking questions in such a direct and challenging manner, they become more motivated to listen.
Your students must feel your weighty eyes upon them. They must feel the urgency to prove how well they listened.

Questions that challenge students and target the pride living inside each of them have great power. They unseat lazy thinking patterns, inspire personal responsibility, and jump start motivational engines.
